$comment: The third review of the interpolation judgement, judged by both editors alike: a call to one of Streamlord's helpers is only the author's own when its arguments are, a nested template is as weak as its holes, qualified constants and enum entries, values joined with + at a DSL expression site, interpolate escaping markup held as a String, the rewrite to interpolate and its per cent signs, Trusted as a fix in element text, and messages that say what helps. A case may give `constants`, the workspace's const val names.

cases.name: a helper call with a String argument is that String: signal(q) in data-text
cases.source:
import io.github.markusaugust.streamlord.html.*
fun f(q: String) = elements { div { dataText("${signal(q)}") } }

issues.message: Kotlin writes ${signal(q)} into data-text, which Datastar runs as an expression or follows as a signal path. Text from outside becomes code there, even inside quotes. Put the value in a signal, or in an attribute of its own read with el.dataset; only a number or a boolean is safe to write in.

cases.name: post(q) at the start of a URL is a String
cases.source: import io.github.markusaugust.streamlord.html.* fun f(q: String) = "x"

issues.message: Kotlin writes ${post(q)} at the start of href, so the value decides the scheme, and a javascript: URL runs. Escaping does not help: start the value with /, # or https://, or build the string with interpolate(...), which refuses a scheme that runs.
fixes: import io.github.markusaugust.streamlord.html.* import io.github.markusaugust.streamlord.core.domain.interpolate fun f(q: String) = interpolate("x", post(q)).text
